sections.title_en: 1. The Mitzva of Tefillin
sections.body_en:
It is a positive commandment from the Torah to bind the hand tefillin on the arm every day, and a further mitzva to bind the head tefillin on the head, in order always to remember the foundations of faith. In the tefillin one places four passages in which the command to put on tefillin appears, and they are: 'Kadesh' (Shemot 13:1-10), 'Ve-haya ki yevi'akha' (there 11-16), 'Shema' (Devarim 6:4-9), 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' (there 11:13-21).1

In these four passages the principles of Israel's faith and Torah are mentioned. In the first two passages the subjects of the sanctity of the firstborn, the Land of Israel, the exodus from Egypt and the festival of Pesaḥ are explained. These foundations express the holiness and special character of Israel, for which God took us out of Egypt with signs and wonders, and in the course of this it was revealed to us and to the world that God oversees the whole world and everything is in His hand. There is great importance to the mitzva of sanctifying the firstborn of man and beast, because it establishes the awareness that everything begins from God, and in order to draw the word of God into the world one must sanctify the beginning of everything (Peninei Halakha, Mishpaḥa 9:1; Pesaḥ 13:3; Kashrut 19:4-8). From this, when we come to the good land, we will draw God's blessing to all creatures and deeds.

In the last two passages in the tefillin the foundations of Israel's faith and their destiny are explained. In the passage of 'Shema' appear the basic mitzvot incumbent on each and every individual: faith in the unity of God and loving Him with all the heart and soul, as it is said (Devarim 6:4-8): "Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might." So that faith will guide our lives, we were commanded to meditate on the Torah day and night and to pass it on to our children after us. In the last passage, 'Ve-haya im shamo'a', the great destiny of the people of Israel to inherit the good land, to keep all the mitzvot in it and to enjoy the Divine blessing is explained. The principle of reward and punishment is also explained in it: that God oversees Israel, and if we sin we will perish from the good land, and if we listen to the voice of God we will be blessed and live long on the land which God swore to our forefathers.

It is a mitzva to put on tefillin every day except Shabbat and festival days, on which the holiness of the day takes the place of the holiness of the tefillin (below halakha 14). The Sages said (Rosh Hashana 17a) that one who sins and does not put on tefillin all his days is the distinct example of "the sinners of Israel with their body". He is the one called "a skull that has not put on tefillin", that is, a head that has never put on tefillin. And his punishment is severe in the World to Come, since he neglected the mitzva that binds his body to holiness. Many hold that even one who did not put on tefillin for one day out of contempt for the mitzva is considered 'a skull that has not put on tefillin'.2

notes_en.en: In all of them the command to put them on the hand and on the head is stated. In 'Kadesh' it is said (Shemot 13:9): "And it shall be for a sign to you upon your hand and for a memorial between your eyes, so that the Torah of the Lord may be in your mouth, for with a strong hand the Lord brought you out of Egypt." In 'Ve-haya ki yevi'akha' it is said (there 16): "And it shall be for a sign upon your hand and for frontlets between your eyes, for with strength of hand the Lord brought us out of Egypt." In 'Shema' it is said (Devarim 6:8): "And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes." And in 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' it is said (there 11:18): "And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes."

Some say that only one who has not put on tefillin all his days is called a sinner of Israel with his body, since their reading of the Gemara is: 'a skull that has never put on tefillin'. And so wrote the Rif, the Rambam (Repentance 3:5), the Ramban, the Ittur and others. And many do not read 'never', and in their view one who out of disdain refrains from putting on tefillin even for one day, for example because the mitzva is contemptible to him, is considered 'a skull that has not put on tefillin' and a sinner of Israel with his body (Rabbeinu Tam in Tosafot, Shabbat 49a, s.v. 'Ke-Elisha'; Hagahot Maimoniyot; the Rashba; the Ritva; the Ran, and others). Similarly it emerges from Rabbeinu Tam that one who refrains for one day from putting on tefillin out of laziness is not a sinner of Israel with his body, because he does not do so in rebellion and contempt. And so wrote the Yere'im 399 and Ha-Manhig (Laws of Tefillin, p. 598). And some say that even one who out of laziness did not put on tefillin for one day is called a sinner of Israel with his body, but if he did not put them on because he feared he would not succeed in guarding their sanctity, although he is mistaken, he is not considered a sinner (the Baḥ; and so the Birkei Yosef 37:1 learned from the words of the Rosh, and it was brought in the Mishna Berura 37:3).
However, there were those in Israel who almost did not put on tefillin, and the Sages said that an am ha-aretz is one who does not put on tefillin (Berakhot 47b; Sota 22a). And the Sages likewise said (Shabbat 130a): "Every mitzva for which Israel did not give themselves over to death at the time of the decree of the government, such as tefillin, is still weak in their hands." And so it emerges from the words of Geonim and Rishonim that there were places in which for generations they almost did not keep the mitzva of tefillin. And R. Moshe of Coucy, the author of the Semag (positive commandments 3), set out on a journey of awakening from France to Spain in order to awaken the many to keep the mitzva. And there were those who explained their negligence in the mitzva by the fear that they would not succeed in guarding their body and thoughts properly, but according to halakha this fear does not exempt from tefillin (Sefer Ha-Ḥinukh 421; Kad Ha-Kemaḥ, Tefillin). See below in halakhot 15-16.

sections.title_en: 2. The Intention of the Mitzva and Its Meaning
sections.body_en:
All the mitzvot require intention, that the one who performs them intend to fulfil the commandment of God (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 60:4). Regarding the mitzva of tefillin the Torah added and explained its purpose, as it is said (Shemot 13:9): "And it shall be for a sign to you upon your hand and for a memorial between your eyes, so that the Torah of the Lord may be in your mouth, for with a strong hand the Lord brought you out of Egypt." Therefore: "When putting them on he should intend that the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded us to put these four passages, which contain the unity of His Name and the exodus from Egypt, on the arm opposite the heart and on the head opposite the brain, so that we remember the miracles and wonders that He did with us, which indicate His unity and that He has the power and dominion over the upper and lower realms to do with them as He wills; and he should subjugate to the Holy One, blessed be He, the soul which is in the brain, and also the heart, which is the essence of the desires and thoughts; and in this way he will remember the Creator and reduce his pleasures" (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 25:5). After the fact, even one who put on tefillin without thinking of this has fulfilled his obligation, since by the very fact that he put on tefillin and recited the blessing over them he intended to fulfil the commandment of God (Mishna Berura 25:15).

Some enhance the mitzva by saying the 'Le-shem yiḥud' formula before putting on the tefillin, in order to express in detail the intentions of the tefillin. And some enhance it by reading, after putting on tefillin, the passages 'Kadesh' and 'Ve-haya ki yevi'akha', in order actually to remember everything written in the tefillin. The passages 'Shema' and 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' are read in the 'recitation of Shema' (Mishna Berura 25:16).

The tefillin are a 'sign' for Israel, that is, a symbol and mark that expresses their essence. And they have a twofold expression: on the one hand they express our being servants of God who accept His kingship. On the other hand, they are also the glorious crown of Israel, for they express Israel's special ability to bind themselves to God and to reveal His Name in the world. And the two sides complement each other. Through dedicating our powers to the service of God we become free, released from the shackles of the world, and crowned with the holiness of the crown of God's kingship.

The tefillin expose the soul within us, and there is a great need for this, because following the troubles of this world and its temptations a person may forget that he was created in the image of God and sink into the needs of the hour and passing desires. By binding the tefillin, in which are the foundations of faith and Torah, we return and bind ourselves to faith and to the eternal ideas of the Divine Torah. This is what the Sages said (Menaḥot 44a-b): "Whoever puts on tefillin lengthens his days, as it is said (Yeshayahu 38:16): The Lord is upon them; they shall live."

Binding the tefillin on the hand and the head hints at the absolute bond between the people of Israel and God and His Torah. Many peoples have spiritual ideas, but there is no people in the world whose spiritual ideas have held out against enormous and terrible challenges over so long a period as the Torah has been preserved in the people of Israel. There are two reasons for this. The first: only Israel did God choose from all the peoples, and only to Israel did God give His Torah; therefore the ideas of the people of Israel are Divine ideas, as against the human ideas of the other peoples. The second reason, which stems from the first: the bond of the other peoples to their ideas is not as deep and strong as the bond of Israel to the Torah. Therefore there has been no people in the world so many of whose children were ready to give their lives for their faith as in Israel. And there is no people in the world in which the Divine matter grips the hearts and minds of so many of its children.

These ideas are expressed by the mitzva of tefillin, in which we bind, quite literally, the passages of the tefillin, in which are written the foundations of faith in God and of the sacred destiny of Israel, on the hand and on the head. By this we bind the main powers in a person, the intellect, the emotion and the deed, to holiness. The hand tefillin are opposite the heart and the hand, which symbolise the emotion and the deed, and the head tefillin are opposite the intellect. In this respect the tefillin express the bond between Israel and God more than the other mitzvot.

sections.title_en: 3. The Mitzva of Putting On Tefillin
sections.body_en:
The obligation from the Torah is to put on tefillin every day for one moment. And one who did not put them on during the whole day has neglected eight positive commandments (Menaḥot 44a), since in each of the four passages of the tefillin a mitzva was stated to put it in the hand tefillin and a mitzva to put it in the head tefillin.

The Sages ruled to put on tefillin at the time of the morning prayer, and especially when saying the recitation of Shema, in which the mitzva of tefillin is written. And they said (Berakhot 14b): "Whoever recites the Shema without tefillin is as if he bears false witness about himself." They further said: "One who wants to accept upon himself the complete yoke of the kingdom of Heaven should relieve himself, wash his hands, put on tefillin, recite the Shema and pray, and this is the complete kingdom of Heaven." And one who does so, "Scripture considers it as if he built an altar and offered a sacrifice on it" (there 15a).

Although in one moment each day one can fulfil the mitzva of tefillin, in every additional moment that a person wears tefillin he fulfils a mitzva from the Torah. In the days of the Mishna and the Gemara many were accustomed to wear tefillin all day, and when they needed to relieve themselves they would remove them and immediately afterwards put them on again. But from the days of the Rishonim until our day the guidance is to fulfil the mitzva of tefillin during the morning prayer and no more (Shulḥan Arukh 37:2). This is because one who wears tefillin must take care not to divert his attention from them and to keep his body clean (below 15-16), and if people wore tefillin all day, it is almost certain that there would be those who would not succeed in guarding their sanctity. And indeed there are those who can guard this, but when only the righteous wear tefillin, a door will be opened thereby for deceivers to cheat people by wearing tefillin and posing as righteous. Therefore everyone became accustomed to wear tefillin only in the morning prayer and the learning after it. And some put on tefillin also in the afternoon prayer.

So at first they used to enhance the mitzva more in the length of time tefillin were worn, even though as a result the tefillin were often treated with disrespect. Later they preferred to enhance it more in guarding their honour than in the length of time tefillin are worn.3

notes_en.en:
It is agreed that whenever a person wears tefillin he fulfils a mitzva from the Torah, and therefore one who removes them and puts them on again must recite the blessing over the mitzva again (below halakha 11). Some add and say that there is a mitzva to wear tefillin all day long, just as it is a mitzva to learn Torah all day long (Rabbeinu Yona; Levush 37:2; the Shela; Peri Ḥadash; Gra 38:10; Yeshu'ot Yaakov, Oraḥ Ḥayim 37:1; and so they learned from the Ramban and Rashba on Shabbat 49a). On the other hand, many hold that the mitzva is to wear tefillin one moment a day, and beyond that it is a measure of piety (Ritva, Shabbat 49a; 130a; Kol Bo; Kesef Mishneh on Foundations of the Torah 5:1 and Leḥem Mishneh there 4; Peri Megadim, Eshel Avraham 37:2; Magen Giborim; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 3; Eshel Avraham of Buczacz 25:1).
In the period of the Mishna and the Gemara many were accustomed to wear tefillin all day long. Therefore the Sages detailed various laws regarding removing the tefillin before entering the lavatory and before a meal (Berakhot 23a-b), and they praised one who was careful not to walk four amot without tefillin (Sukka 28a; Ta'anit 20b; Megilla 28a). On the other hand, from the period of the Mishna until the Rishonim there were those who did not put on tefillin at all. Some of them claimed that they did so out of fear that they would not succeed in guarding their sanctity (above note 2). And the Rishonim wrote to put them on only in the morning prayer, because tefillin require a clean body and care against diverting attention, and it is hard to guard this for long hours, but at the time of prayer it is possible (Rosh, Tefillin 28; Semak 153; Shulḥan Arukh 37:2).
They said in the Yerushalmi (Berakhot 2:3; Pesikta Rabbati 22) that people are not accustomed to wear tefillin all day because of the deceivers, who would pose as righteous by means of the tefillin and deceive people into giving them money, and afterwards betray their trust. And so wrote Rabbeinu Yeruḥam (Toledot Adam Ve-Ḥava, path 19:5), and the Magen Avraham (37:2): "Even one who knows of himself that he has a clean body should not wear them all day, because of the deceivers." And so wrote the Eliya Rabba 37:2. On the other hand, according to the Ri (Tosafot, Shabbat 49a, s.v. 'Ke-Elisha') and the Rosh (Hilkhot Ketanot, Tefillin 28), the intention of the Yerushalmi is that one should not trust one who wears tefillin all day, but they did not mean to rule that one should not wear tefillin all day. And the Gra (Ma'ase Rav 18) wrote that one who can keep himself in cleanliness must wear tefillin all day, and if he is concerned about arrogance he should wear the hand tefillin only, and it is preferable that he make small head tefillin that he can conceal. And his words were brought in the Bi'ur Halakha (37:2, s.v. 'Mitzvatan').
Torah study and tefillin: the Sages said (Mekhilta de-Rabbi Yishmael, Bo 17): "Whoever reads in the Torah is exempt from tefillin", that is, from wearing them all day. For the purpose of putting on tefillin is "so that the Torah of the Lord may be in your mouth" (Shemot 13:9), and one who learns Torah fulfils this in practice. But at the time of the recitation of Shema one must put on tefillin; and so wrote Rabbeinu Yona, the Mordekhai and the Shulḥan Arukh (38:10). However, in the Pesikta Zutrata (Parashat Bo 13:9) it is explained that even one who learns Torah is commanded to put on tefillin. And so wrote Rav Shmuel bar Ḥofni Gaon, the Agur and the Tur (38:10). And in the view of the Ittur, the words of the Mekhilta were said of one who reads Scripture, but one who learns Talmud must put on tefillin, and his words were brought in the Rosh, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and the Magen Avraham (38:13).

sections.title_en: 4. The Place of the Hand Tefillin
sections.body_en:
The place of the hand tefillin is on the swelling muscle of the arm, with a slight inclination inwards towards the heart. As it is said in the passage of 'Shema' (Devarim 6:8): "And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand", and likewise it is said in the passage of 'Ve-haya im shamo'a' (Devarim 11:18): "And you shall put these my words upon your heart and upon your soul, and bind them for a sign upon your hand." From this the Sages learned (Menaḥot 37b) that one must put the tefillin on the highest place of the arm, and in this way the tefillin will be upon the arm. And one cannot say that the intention is to put them on the palm of the hand, because the Torah compared the hand tefillin to the head tefillin, and just as the head tefillin are at the height of the head, so the hand tefillin must be at the height of the arm. And one cannot say that the intention is to put them on the shoulder, because then they would already be outside the arm. Rather, the intention is to bind them on the most raised place of the arm, which is the place of the kibboret, that is, the prominent muscle between the shoulder and the elbow. In addition, it is said to put the tefillin "upon your heart", that is, on the muscle of the arm which is opposite the heart. We further learned from this that it is right to incline the tefillin slightly towards the side of the heart, but one should not incline them much, because then the tefillin will not be on the muscle.

As a reason for the mitzva one can say that binding the hand tefillin is meant to hint two things to us. The first: that above all the mighty deeds a person does with his hands and muscles stands faith in the One who gave us the strength to achieve all this valour. The second: that the heart, with all its emotional power, must be directed and guided by the Torah; therefore we put the tefillin on the muscle of the arm and opposite the heart.

Some say that not every part of the muscle is valid for tefillin, but only the part of the muscle that is on the lower half of the bone between the elbow and the shoulder. But almost all the Rishonim did not mention this; rather, they wrote that the tefillin must be on the 'kibboret' (the muscle) and opposite the heart. However, since many Aḥaronim took into account the view that the place of the tefillin is on the lower half of the bone, ideally it is right to act according to them. And one should measure the bone from the shoulder to the elbow, and the place of the muscle is measured when the arm is straight, so that a considerable majority of the muscle is indeed in the lower half of the bone. And one who has difficulty putting them on the lower half, because he has a wound there or because he is a youth whose arm is short and his tefillin are large, should put the tefillin on with a blessing on the place of the muscle, even above the lower half of the bone, for the main thing is that all the tefillin rest on the place of the muscle.

It is preferable to cover the hand tefillin, as it is said (Shemot 13:9): "And it shall be for a sign to you upon your hand" – "a sign to you, and not a sign to others" (Menaḥot 37b; Mishna Berura 27:47).4

notes_en.en:
Menaḥot 37b: "The Master said: 'Your hand' – this is the kibboret (the muscle). From where do we know this? For the Rabbis taught: 'upon your hand' – this is the height of the arm. You say this is the height of the arm, or is it rather literally upon your hand? The Torah said: put tefillin on the hand and put tefillin on the head; just as there it is at the height of the head, so here it is at the height of the arm. Rabbi Eliezer says: this is not needed, for it says: 'And it shall be for a sign to you' – a sign to you, and not a sign to others (a place that is usually hidden by the garment). Rabbi Yitzḥak says: this is not needed, for it says: 'And you shall put these my words upon your heart… and bind them' – that the placing be opposite the heart." Further there: "Rabbi Ḥiya and Rav Aḥa son of Rav Avya would aim and place it opposite his heart." From here, one must incline the tefillin slightly towards the side of the heart (Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh 27:1, based on the Rambam and the Rosh). But the inclination is not indispensable (Taharat Ha-Kodesh, Menaḥot 37b).
Rabbeinu Peretz wrote, based on the Shimusha Rabba (Hagahot Semak 153), that the tefillin should be put on the half of the arm towards the elbow. His words were brought as halakha in the Agudda, the Mordekhai and the Kol Bo, the Shulḥan Arukh (27:7) and the Rema (27:1). And so wrote many Aḥaronim, among them: the Levush (27:1), Magen Avraham 2, Olat Tamid 1, Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 2, Artzot Ha-Ḥayim 1. And some even wrote not to recite the blessing if they are on the upper half (Ḥayei Adam 14:10; Yeḥaveh Da'at 5:3). And some even wrote that one may put them on the lower half where it is not on the muscle (Levush 27:1).
But there is a difficulty, for the other Rishonim who preceded Rabbeinu Peretz did not mention this matter, but only that the place of the tefillin is on the kibboret. And Rabbeinu Ḥananel (Eruvin 95b) even wrote that the place is in the middle of the arm. A further difficulty: the heart is not opposite the lower half of the arm, but opposite the middle of the arm or a little higher. A further difficulty: Rabbeinu Peretz wrote his words simply without explaining the source of his novel ruling. A further difficulty: the Sages said that there is room on the arm to put two tefillin, and according to Rabbeinu Peretz there is no room there for that, especially according to the Shimusha Rabba, who holds that the tefillin must be large (the housing at least two fingers, below 4, note 3). A further difficulty: in young youths the lower half is outside the muscle, and this is indispensable according to the plain meaning of the Gemara and most poskim (so wrote the Beit Yosef in Bedek Ha-Bayit 27:1; Magen Avraham 27:2, and others). Indeed, according to the Gra (27:1; Ma'ase Rav, Tefillin 21), Rabbeinu Peretz should not be taken into account at all, and what he brought in the name of the Shimusha Rabba means that one must put the tefillin on the muscle, whose length is about half the arm, in its middle. And the view of most Aḥaronim is that the main halakha is that the place of the tefillin is on the muscle, and although ideally one should take into account the view of Rabbeinu Peretz and put them on the lower half, when there is difficulty in this one should put them on even on the upper half with a blessing, provided that it is on the kibboret. So wrote many, among them: Ha'amek She'ala (145:3), Mishna Berura 4, Ben Ish Ḥai (Ḥayei Sara 6). And so is the custom, not to be very concerned about the view of Rabbeinu Peretz (see Ma'adanei Shlomo, Tefillin 2). (According to the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 27:4, when necessary one should put them on the upper part even where it is not on the muscle.)
And it appears that Rabbeinu Peretz meant to explain what is understood and agreed, and since he did not see in it a novelty he did not need to give reasons for his words. And his intention is that the place of the kibboret is in the lower half of the whole bone, that is, the bone that extends from the shoulder to the elbow. And the place of the kibboret is when the arm is straight, which is the usual position of the arm, and then the place of the muscle is longer (Oraḥ Mishpat 4). And one cannot argue that the bone must be measured from the armpit, for when one raises the arm the same measure comes out between the elbow and the centre of the armpit. In this way it emerges that the main place of the kibboret is in the lower half and opposite the heart. And so emerges from the words of Rabbeinu Peretz himself in his Tosafot (Eruvin 95b): "Their place is from half the arm to the elbow, which is the 'kuda', and this is half the arm, and this is what it says, 'your hand' is the kibboret, meaning the flesh gathered between the elbow and the shoulder." So in his view the place of the muscle corresponds to his definition, half the arm. And so the Bi'ur Halakha learned (27:1, s.v. 'Be-rosh ha-etzem') from the words of the Terumah, that the lower half and the place of the kibboret are one place. In this way the main difficulties against Rabbeinu Peretz are resolved (and so wrote Ḥut Shani 27:3). However, there is still a difficulty, that there is a little muscle in the upper half, and it may be that he did not mean to measure the bone precisely but to explain that in general it is the lower half.
As said above, in the Gemara Menaḥot (37b) the place of the tefillin is in a place that is usually covered, but there is no obligation to cover the hand tefillin, for the main thing is that it be in a place that is usually concealed. And so wrote the Rema (27:11). But it is better to cover it (the Terumah; Levush 27:11; Mishna Berura 47).

sections.title_en: 5. The Straps and Interposition
sections.body_en:
Binding the tefillin to the hand and the head is done by means of the tefillin straps, and it is a halakha given to Moshe at Sinai to dye them black, and people are particular that when binding the tefillin the black colour faces outwards (Shulḥan Arukh 27:11).

The length of the hand strap is enough to bind the tefillin with it on the muscle of the arm, and from there it continues to the middle finger, around which it is wound three times. And the custom is to wind the strap around the forearm seven times, and to wind it on the palm and the fingers in the shapes of 'shin' and 'yud' (below 4:6).

The custom is that the straps of the head tefillin hang down in front of him, with the right strap reaching to the place of circumcision and the left to the navel (below 4:6). By this one draws the influence of holiness on the right side down to the place of the covenant and procreation, and on the left side down to the place where food is digested.

The correct custom is that the ma'abarta, through which the strap passes, be on the side of the shoulder, and in this way the tefillin will be well bound to the arm (Shulḥan Arukh 27:3).

One must take care that there be nothing interposing between the tefillin and the body; that is, one should not put the hand tefillin on the sleeve or the head tefillin on a hat, even if it is thin. But one who had a wound at the place of the tefillin and needed to put a bandage on it should put the tefillin on it without a blessing, since some hold that a bandage does not interpose (Shulḥan Arukh 27:5; Magen Avraham 8).

Ideally people are particular that there be no interposition under the straps that bind and fasten the tefillin to the arm and the head either, but after the fact interposition under the straps does not invalidate, and one puts them on over it with a blessing (Levush; Mishna Berura 27:16). By the letter of the law there may be interposition at the place of the seven windings on the forearm, since they do not bind the tefillin to the arm. But many are accustomed to enhance the mitzva and remove interposition from the place of the windings too, and therefore people are accustomed to remove the watch from the arm before putting on tefillin (Peri Megadim, Mishbetzot Zahav 4).5

notes_en.en:
In Zevaḥim (19a) it is explained that there may be no interposition between the flesh of the kohen and his garments, and therefore the kohanim may not put on tefillin during their service. So one may not put tefillin on the sleeve of the shirt, for if it were permitted the kohanim could put them on over their garments. The Rosh (Responsa 3:4) further learned from this that there may also be no interposition between the head and the tefillin. And so wrote the Yere'im 399, Responsa Ritva 24 and the Tashbetz (1:30). On the other hand, according to the Rashba (3:282), the law of interposition applies only to the hand, as it is said, "a sign to you and not a sign to others", but on the head there is no law of interposition, since the head tefillin must be seen, as it is said (Devarim 28:10): "And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the name of the Lord is called upon you, and they shall be afraid of you", and therefore one may put them on a hat. And so wrote the Ran (Megilla 15b in the pages of the Rif).
In practice, the poskim ruled to be stringent according to the Rosh and those with him, except that one who because of circumstances beyond his control cannot put the tefillin on the head itself should put them on a hat or bandage without a blessing (Responsa Rivash 137; Shulḥan Arukh and Rema 27:4-5). One whose hair has fallen out and who goes with a wig and is embarrassed to remove it during prayer should put on tefillin at home with a blessing without the wig, and afterwards in the synagogue he should put the tefillin on over the wig without a blessing (Igrot Moshe 4, 40:18).
Regarding a bandage on the arm at the place of the tefillin, some say that since it is a necessity it does not interpose, and therefore one should put the hand tefillin on over the bandage without a blessing (Magen Avraham 27:8 and Mishna Berura 18).
The hair of the head does not interpose, even if it is long like the hair of a lifelong nazir. However, in the Maḥatzit Ha-Shekel (27:4) he wrote that one who grows a forelock sins through haughtiness and pride, and in addition, there is a concern that his hair interposes before the tefillin. And the Mishna Berura 15 brought this. But their words cannot be accepted, since the nezirim grew their hair and put on tefillin. Also among those mourning for parents there are those who were accustomed not to cut their hair for many months, up to a year, and they certainly put on tefillin (Mor U-Ketzi'a; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 27:14; Or Le-Tziyon 2, 44:19; Benei Banim 1:6; Yeḥaveh Da'at 2:2; and see there 3:2 regarding a watch).

sections.title_en: 6. The 'Yud' Knot, and One Who Cannot Put Them On Himself
sections.body_en:
A knot in the shape of 'yud' is made from the strap of the hand tefillin (below 4:6). The knot must be on the side of the heart, and it is right that it be close to the tefillin. According to the custom of those of Sephardi origin and many of those of Ashkenazi origin, the winding of the straps of the hand tefillin is outwards. In this way the 'yud' knot is always drawn towards the housing of the tefillin and remains close to it. But according to the custom of some of those of Ashkenazi origin, the winding is inwards, and in this way the 'yud' knot often moves away from the housing of the tefillin. In practice, however, even if the 'yud' knot does not touch the housing of the tefillin, one has fulfilled the mitzva (Shulḥan Arukh 27:2).6

One whose hands have become weak and who cannot put on tefillin by himself must find someone who will bind the tefillin for him, and in this way he can fulfil the mitzva and recite the blessing. His wife or daughter or a minor or even a gentile may do this, because the mitzva is not to bind the tefillin but that the tefillin be bound on the hand and the head. As it is said (Shemot 13:9): "And it shall be for a sign to you upon your hand and for a memorial between your eyes, so that the Torah of the Lord may be in your mouth, for with a strong hand the Lord brought you out of Egypt." And what is said, 'and you shall bind them for a sign', means that through the binding the tefillin will be a sign, but not that the binding itself is the mitzva.7

notes_en.en:
Menaḥot 35b: "The knot of the tefillin… must be facing inwards, so that Israel will be inwards and not outwards." Many learned from this that the 'yud' knot must be towards the heart. So wrote Rav Amram Gaon and Rav Hai Gaon, the Or Zarua (1:576), the Rosh (Tefillin 12), and others. There were indeed those who were accustomed to have the knot on the outer side, but the halakha was decided that it should be facing inwards (Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh 27:2).
The Shulḥan Arukh (27:2) wrote, based on the Zohar (III 236b): "One must take care that the yud of the knot does not move away from the tefillin." Most Aḥaronim copied the wording of the Shulḥan Arukh, and plainly the intention is to fasten the knot close to the titura, and so several Aḥaronim wrote explicitly (Ḥesed La-Alafim 25:10; Avnei Nezer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 14). And some are meticulous to fasten the knot specifically to the ketzitza. And according to the Teshurat Shai (second edition 93), as long as the knot is close to the tefillin, even if there is air between them, it is considered fastened to it. However, those who follow the Kabbala are more careful about this, and one of the reasons for winding the straps on the housing of the tefillin according to the custom of the kabbalists is in order to fasten the knot to the housing (Birkei Yosef 25:9). And some are even more meticulous and tie the knot to the housing of the tefillin with a sinew (Ben Ish Ḥai, Vayera 15). But the custom of Israel is not to add tyings with sinews and the like (see Sha'arei Teshuva 5; Mishna Berura 10).
Sometimes a left-handed person needs to borrow tefillin from a right-handed one or vice versa, and then a problem arises, because the knot of the tefillin must be on the side of the heart, and the ma'abarta through which the strap passes must be on the side of the shoulder (Shulḥan Arukh 27:2-3), and if a left-handed person takes the tefillin of a right-handed person it is impossible for the ma'abarta to be on top and the knot on the side of the heart. And the Bi'ur Halakha wrote (27:3, s.v. 'Ha-minhag'), based on the Shevut Yaakov and the Artzot Ha-Ḥayim, that the more important law is that the knot be on the side of the heart, for it is the law of the Gemara, whereas the ma'abarta facing upwards is a custom about which there is no strictness (Terumat Ha-Deshen 49). And it is right that he wind the strap also around the upper side of the tefillin in order to bind them well to the arm. The Ḥayei Adam indeed proposed taking the strap out and reversing it, but the Bi'ur Halakha has doubts about this. In addition, reversing the strap may cause some damage to the straps and to how tightly the knot is fastened to the tefillin, and for this reason too it is right to act according to the words of the Bi'ur Halakha.
One accustomed to wind the tefillin outwards, as the Sephardi custom, who borrowed tefillin from one accustomed to wind inwards, as the Ashkenazi custom, or the reverse, should not reverse the tefillin, for then the 'yud' would be far from the heart; rather he should put them on according to the custom of the owner of the tefillin. For these customs are not mentioned in the Gemara or the Rishonim, and both are good, and there is no reason to be particular to keep them when borrowing tefillin. And if he wishes, he can wind half a turn around the ketzitza and thereby change the direction of the strap outwards.

A woman may bind tefillin for her husband, as brought in Avoda Zara (39a): "And so Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar used to say: It once happened that a certain woman married a ḥaver, and she would bind tefillin on his arm…" And so wrote Mahari Assad (Yehuda Ya'ale, Oraḥ Ḥayim 19), Maharam Schick (Oraḥ Ḥayim 15) and Yabi'a Omer (9, Oraḥ Ḥayim 7:2) (although in Teshurat Shai, first edition 618, he was stringent that the one who binds must be obligated in the mitzva). And the same law applies to a gentile, who may put tefillin on a Jew who needs this (Maharshag 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 9; Ashrei Ha-Ish, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1, Tefillin 17; Mekor Ne'eman 2:97).

sections.title_en: 7. The Left Hand
sections.body_en:
The tefillin are put on the left arm, for it is said (Devarim 6:8): "And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand", and 'hand' unqualified in Tanakh is the left hand, as it is said (Shofetim 5:26): "She put her hand to the tent peg, and her right hand to the workmen's hammer." It is further said (Devarim 6:8-9): "And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand, and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes. And you shall write them upon the doorposts of your house and upon your gates." The Sages learned that the right hand, which is used for writing the mezuzot, is the one that must bind the tefillin on the left hand. The Sages further interpreted from what is said (Shemot 13:16): "And it shall be for a sign upon your hand (yadkhah)", with an added 'heh', that one must put the tefillin on the 'keha' (weaker) hand, that is, on the weak hand (Menaḥot 37a). If one deviated and put the tefillin on the right hand, he has not fulfilled his obligation (Mishna Berura 27:1). However, a left-handed person puts them on his right hand, because it is his weak hand, as explained in the next halakha.

As a reason for the mitzva to put the tefillin on the weak hand, one can explain that the weak hand expresses the less good sides of the actions of the hands, and therefore specifically on it we were commanded to put the tefillin, in order to sanctify it and bind it to faith and the love of God.

One whose left arm was amputated, as long as the place of the muscle on which tefillin are put remains, should put on tefillin with a blessing (for more details see the note).

A right-handed person whose right hand was amputated or became ill and weak, since his strong hand is now the left, should put tefillin on his right hand, which has become his weaker hand (Dagul Me-Revava 27:6; Mishna Berura 22).8

notes_en.en:
Menaḥot (37a): "Others say: 'your hand' – to include one whose hand is cut off." That is, one whose left hand was amputated but the kibboret on which tefillin are put remains is obligated in tefillin. According to Tosafot (s.v. 'Ein lo'), there is no other view in the Gemara. On the other hand, according to the Or Zarua (1:577), in the view of the first Tanna in the baraita there, one whose arm was amputated up to the elbow, even though the place of the kibboret remains, is exempt from tefillin, since the obligation of putting them on applies to an ordinary, whole arm. And the Rema (27:1) took his view into account, and therefore wrote that one whose left arm was amputated up to the elbow should put tefillin on it without a blessing. And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 3 and Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 9. But many disagreed with the Rema and hold that if the place of the kibboret on the left arm remains, one is obligated to put tefillin on it with a blessing. So wrote the Baḥ, Eliya Rabba, Gra 1, Torat Ḥayim Sofer 1, Ḥavot Ya'ir 167, and the Bi'ur Halakha brought them (s.v. 'Be-lo berakha'). And I wrote above that he should recite the blessing on putting on the hand tefillin (unlike the Bi'ur Halakha there), because this is the main view. And there is no concern of a blessing in vain if he does so, for even according to the Or Zarua one must recite a blessing over the head tefillin, and if he recites it over the hand tefillin, all that will result according to the Or Zarua is an unnecessary interruption between the blessing and the time it takes effect on the head tefillin, but after the fact the blessing will take effect. (That is, according to the Rema 26:2, following the Or Zarua he should recite two blessings over the head tefillin, and it is preferable that he follow the main view and recite 'le-haniaḥ' over the hand tefillin and 'al mitzvat' over the head. And according to the Shulḥan Arukh 26:2, following the Or Zarua he would need to recite 'al mitzvat' over the head tefillin, and according to the main view he must recite 'le-haniaḥ' over the hand tefillin and thereby exempt the head tefillin too. And since after the fact one may recite 'le-haniaḥ' over the head tefillin, it emerges that according to the Or Zarua there is no concern of a blessing in vain, and consequently it is right to follow the main view.)
If his left arm was amputated including the place of the kibboret, he is exempt from tefillin (Or Zarua; Shiltei Ha-Gibborim; Responsa Rema 122; Baḥ; Magen Avraham 3, and others. And so it is implied by Tosafot, the Agudda and the Riaz. However, according to the Maharshal he should put them on the right arm. And the Artzot Ha-Ḥayim 1 and Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 5 wrote to put them on the right arm without a blessing).
One born without a left arm is plainly exempt from the hand tefillin, but several poskim wrote that he should put them on his right arm without a blessing (Shevut Yaakov 1:3; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 7). One born without a right arm puts them on the left arm with a blessing (this is plain, and so wrote the Tzemaḥ Tzedek, Oraḥ Ḥayim 5).
It is explained above that if his right hand was amputated or became ill and weak, he has become left-handed; so wrote the Tzitz Eliezer (16:17), Yabi'a Omer (9, Oraḥ Ḥayim 7), and others (and see Tzemaḥ Tzedek 5, and Minḥat Shlomo 2:4-5). Similarly we learned in the Mordekhai (Menaḥot 969, brought in the Beit Yosef 27:6) that some say that one who trains himself to be left-handed should nevertheless put them on the left hand, for originally it was his weak hand. But in practice he ruled to follow the actual situation, and since he has become left-handed he should put them on the right. Thus far. And so wrote the Magen Avraham 9 and the Mishna Berura 22. The Dagul Me-Revava (27:6) added that even according to those who hold that one does not take into account a person's having changed his nature, when the change was made by Heaven one follows the situation that was brought about by the change.

sections.title_en: 8. The Law of a Left-Handed Person
sections.body_en:
A left-handed person puts tefillin on his right hand, because it is his weak hand. However, in the view of the Meiri and several of the kabbalists, a left-handed person too puts them on the left, since the place of the tefillin is opposite the heart (above halakha 4), and the place of the heart is on the left side. But in the view of almost all the poskim, a left-handed person must put them on the right hand, for the mitzva is not to put them on the left hand but on the weak hand, and since for a left-handed person the weak hand is the right, it is on it that he must put the tefillin. However, one who is ambidextrous puts tefillin on his left, like most people (Menaḥot 37b).

The poskim disagreed about one who writes with one hand while his other hand is the strong one. Some say that he puts them on the weak hand (the Rosh, the Gra, Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 27:16). And some say that he puts them on the hand he does not write with (Shulḥan Arukh 27:6; Magen Avraham; Ḥayei Adam; Yabi'a Omer 6, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2). And some say that whenever he writes with his right hand, or it is his strong hand, or he does several important tasks with it, he is considered ambidextrous and should put them on the left hand (Tosafot, the Baḥ, the Artzot Ha-Ḥayim and the Ben Ish Ḥai). And so it appears in practice. But it is fitting for one who has a rabbi to act as his rabbi instructs him.9

notes_en.en:
In the baraita (Menaḥot 36b-37a) three sources were mentioned for putting the tefillin on the left hand: "The Rabbis taught: 'your hand' – this is the left. You say the left, or is it rather the right? Scripture says: 'My hand also laid the foundation of the earth, and My right hand spread out the heavens', and it says: 'She put her hand to the tent peg, and her right hand to the workmen's hammer'… Rabbi Natan says: this is not needed, for it says 'and you shall bind them' and 'and you shall write them': just as writing is with the right hand, so binding is with the right hand, and since binding is with the right, putting them on is on the left… Rav Ashi said: 'yadkhah' is written with a heh, 'keha' (weak)." Further there: "The Rabbis taught: a left-handed person puts tefillin on his right, which is his left. But it was taught: he puts them on his left, which is the left of every person! Abaye said: when that was taught, it was about one who is ambidextrous." Some say that a left-handed person too must put them on the left hand. So wrote the Meiri (Shabbat 103a), because there is a further derivation (Menaḥot 37b) that the tefillin must be opposite the heart, which leans to the left, and the Ḥatan Sofer learned similarly (Sha'ar Ha-Totefet 28). And so wrote Mahari Tzemaḥ (Zer Zahav, Oraḥ Ḥayim 27:3), that according to the esoteric teaching one must always put them on the left hand. That is, they ruled like the first Tanna, who learned that 'hand' unqualified is the left.
But almost all the poskim hold that a left-handed person must put them on the right, and they disagreed about one who writes with one hand while his other hand is the strong one. Some say that he should put them on his weak hand, and writing is not taken into account (the Terumah, the Mordekhai and the Rosh, Tefillin 18; Gra 27:17; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 16). And some say that one follows the writing, and the weak hand is not taken into account (so the Beit Yosef 27:6 understood the words of the Semak and Rabbeinu Yeḥiel). And some say that whether his strong hand is the right or he writes with the right, he is considered ambidextrous and must put them on the left (Rabbeinu Peretz as brought in the Mordekhai, Menaḥot 969; Piskei Tosafot 124, based on Tosafot, Menaḥot 37a, s.v. 'Ma ketiva').
The Shulḥan Arukh (27:6) brought as the first 'some say' that he should put them on the weak hand, and as the second 'some say' that one follows the writing. And according to the rules of the Shulḥan Arukh, his view is like the last 'some say'. And so wrote the Rema, that the custom is to follow the writing. And so wrote the Hagahot Ha-Levush 6, and Eliya Rabba there, Magen Avraham 9, Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 9, Ḥayei Adam (14:11) and Sho'el U-Nish'al (1:3). And so wrote Yabi'a Omer (6, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2), except that he added that because of the doubt, after the prayer he should put them on his other hand too.
But there is a difficulty for those who hold that one who writes with the left hand should put them on the right hand although it is the strong one, for from the Gemara it emerges that there is no dispute between the derivations regarding the law of a left-handed person, which implies that whether he writes with the right hand or the right is his strong hand, he puts them on the left. Further, most of the Rishonim ruled simply that the main thing is to put them on the weak hand; so wrote the She'iltot 45, the Rif (Laws of Tefillin 9a), the Rashba (Ḥullin 92b) and the Ran (there on the Rif). In addition, the Beit Yosef learned the whole basis of the view that one follows the writing from the Semak and Rabbeinu Yeḥiel, but the Baḥ explained that their view is like Tosafot, that whenever he writes with the right or the right is his strong hand, he puts them on the left. And so wrote the Olat Tamid (27:7), the Tzemaḥ Tzedek (Oraḥ Ḥayim 4) and Sho'el U-Meshiv (second edition 3:123). And so wrote Igrot Moshe (Oraḥ Ḥayim 4:11), and he added that it does not stand to reason to rule to satisfy all the views, "for it is a great burden, and we have not found such advice in the books of our Rabbis"; rather, the Sages of the generation must decide how to act.
In addition, some say that even a completely left-handed person who put them on the left has fulfilled his obligation after the fact (Beit Yaakov 149, and Artzot Ha-Ḥayim 27:6, based on the Ba'al Ha-Ittur brought in the Beit Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayim 651:3). However, many hold that he has not fulfilled it (Responsa Ḥut Ha-Shani 28 by the author of the Ḥavot Ya'ir; Sha'arei Teshuva 1; Maharsham 2:240; Mishna Berura 27:24; Bi'ur Halakha, s.v. 'Maniaḥ bi-smolo'. In their view this is also the view of the Ittur). In addition, in the Artzot Ha-Ḥayim (27:6) and in the Ben Ish Ḥai (Ḥayei Sara 7) they brought the words of the kabbalists in the Zer Zahav (27:3), who hold that even a left-handed person must put them on the left. And although they did not rule according to them, they ruled that whether one follows the writing or his strong hand, he should put them on the left hand like every person. And so wrote the Kaf Ha-Ḥayim (27:31).
And so wrote my teacher and rabbi, Rav Mordekhai Eliyahu zt"l, based on their words, in his approbation to 'Peninei Halakha' (5753): "It is fitting to rule that if he does one of the tasks with his right hand, he must put tefillin on his left hand" (and so he wrote in his book Ma'amar Mordekhai for weekdays 8:38). And so it appears in practice, that whenever he writes with his right hand, or it is his strong hand, or he does several important tasks with it, he should put them on the left. For when one examines the words of the Rishonim carefully, one finds that in every situation of doubt, when one rules to put them on the left hand, one rules according to the view of most of the Rishonim. In addition, this is the proper guidance according to the Kabbala. And one may add those who hold that after the fact even a left-handed person who put them on the left has fulfilled the obligation. In addition, in general, in the cases where there is hesitation whether a person is left-handed, it is not common for the division between writing and strength to be sharp, and consequently even those who want to act according to strength or according to writing find themselves in great doubts. For example, one who writes with the left also writes a little with the right hand, or one whose left hand is stronger hammers with his right hand (see Bi'ur Halakha 27:6, s.v. 'Ve-hakhi nahug'); and the Torah did not give its words to measures in which doubts multiply, and the resolution of the doubt is that whenever he is a little right-handed, he is ambidextrous and should put them on the left. In addition, many of those who hold that one who writes with the left should put them on the right agree that if by nature he was right-handed and trained himself to write with the left, he should put them on the left, as the Magen Avraham (27:10) and Mishna Berura 27 wrote. In practice it is hard to know why this person, whose strong hand is the right, writes with the left; perhaps he trained himself to it for an external reason, for example because when he was learning to write he sat next to a child who prevented him from writing with the right, or because at that time his right hand was injured.

sections.title_en: 9. The Place of the Head Tefillin
sections.body_en:
The place for putting on the head tefillin is from the beginning of the area where the hair of the head grows above the forehead up to the place where a baby's skull is soft, that is, the end of the soft area on a baby's head. And one must align the tefillin so that they are in the middle of the head, opposite the space between the eyes (Shulḥan Arukh 27:9-10). If the tefillin are not aligned precisely in the middle of the head but have moved slightly to the right or left, as long as they rest opposite the space between the eyes they are still in their place. Therefore there is no need to use a mirror to align them exactly; it is enough to align them by feeling with the hand (Divrei Ḥayim 2:6; Tzitz Eliezer 12:6:2).

The head tefillin are bound by tightening the straps around the head, with the housing of the tefillin resting on the front of the head, and the knot of the tefillin at the back of the head, at the place where the nape joins the skull. Usually there is a kind of hollow in the nape below the skull, and the knot should be placed at the top of the hollow, so that the straps grip the skull and the tefillin are fastened to the head in the best way.

One must take care that not even part of the tefillin be below the hairline towards the forehead, because in the view of many, even if a little of the tefillin rests opposite the forehead, one has not fulfilled the mitzva and his blessing is in vain. Since the shape of the head is slightly round and the bottom of the tefillin is flat, it turns out that the edge of the tefillin does not actually touch the place where the hair grows; therefore one must make sure that all of the tefillin are opposite the place where the hair grows. There are indeed poskim who hold that it is enough for most of the tefillin to be on the place where the hair grows. But since this is a mitzva from the Torah, and many hold that even if the edge of the tefillin is not over the hairline one has not fulfilled the mitzva, one should be stringent according to them.

A person whose hair grows on the upper part of the forehead should not put them there, but only on top of the head like other people. One who has gone bald over the years should put them on the place where his hair grew when he was young, for the deciding factor is the place where it grows as is usual for most people.

Since every day one tightens the strap around the head, the strap stretches and lengthens out of the knot, and the tefillin tend to slip towards the forehead. Therefore one must check the state of the straps every half year or year. In general, it is preferable that the strap be shorter, so that if it stretches a little the tefillin will still be in their place (Mishna Berura 27:33). It is good that in every synagogue there be someone who knows how to lengthen and shorten the straps, in order to help those praying to fulfil the mitzva.

As a reason for the mitzva one can say that the tefillin must rest on the head in order to express that the source of influence for all our thoughts is from God, who is entirely above us. But if they come down below the hairline, they are no longer entirely above, and since one has not emphasised that the Divine influence is entirely from above, he has not fulfilled the mitzva properly. And the tefillin must be in the middle of the head opposite the space between the eyes, in order to express that the Divine influence comes to us from one source, from the one God. And from this the blessing extends to the different sides, which find expression in the division into two eyes.10

notes_en.en:
In Menaḥot (37a) the Sages said that the place of the head tefillin is at the place where a baby's skull is soft. They further learned there (37b), by a gezera shava from the prohibition of making a bald patch for the dead, that it is at the place where the hair grows at the top of the head. The Rishonim explained (Rosh, Tefillin 18; the Mordekhai; Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and the Terumah) that these places are the boundaries; that is, one must put the head tefillin between the place where a baby's skull is soft and the end of the place where the hair grows. And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (27:9).
In Responsa Beit Yaakov (131) he wrote that it was not explained in the poskim whether the titura too must be above the hairline; according to the Taz only the ketzitza must be on the place of the hair, while the titura may be opposite the forehead; but in his view the titura too must be above the place where the hair grows. According to the Ma'amar Mordekhai 8, the Taz too agrees with the Beit Yaakov that the titura must be on the place of the hair. And according to the Olat Tamid (27:8), only the ketzitza must be on the place of the hair. In practice, many Aḥaronim were not precise about this, among them: Eliya Rabba, Ḥayei Adam, Ḥesed La-Alafim and others. And some wrote explicitly that one must put the tefillin, including the titura, on the place where the hair grows, among them: Peri Megadim (Mishbetzot Zahav 27:10), Shevilei David (27:4), Imrei Yosher Ḥadashot 3, Mishna Berura (27:33), Yeḥaveh Da'at (5:3). Rav Kook in his youth wrote the treatise 'Ḥavash Pe'er' to strengthen sharply the obligation that the titura too be on the place where the hair grows, and since one who does not do so loses the mitzva and recites a blessing in vain, one should point this out to him.
There were, however, those who were accustomed to put part of the tefillin outside the place where the hair grows, as was testified, for example, about the Rebbes of Belz. There are three grounds for this: (a) Some poskim, such as the Taz and the Olat Tamid, hold that the titura need not be on the place where the hair grows. And so wrote the Torat Ḥayim (Sofer 27:10). (b) Some say that it is enough for most of the ketzitza to be above the place where the hair grows (Tiferet Ziv 1:1; Devar Yehoshua 4:11). (c) Some say that whatever is in the air is not counted, and it is enough that the part touching the head be on the place where the hair grows (Devar Yehoshua there; Omer Ve-Da'at 1). And some ruled that ideally one should be particular according to the stringent view, but they found merit for those who are lenient on these grounds, and therefore ruled that one should not point it out to them (Da'at Kedoshim 27:9; Maḥshavot Be-Etza 1).

sections.title_en: 10. Putting On the Tefillin, and Not Interrupting Between Hand and Head
sections.body_en:
One should first bind the hand tefillin and afterwards the head tefillin, as it is said (Devarim 6:8): "And you shall bind them for a sign upon your hand", and afterwards, "and they shall be for frontlets between your eyes" (Menaḥot 36a). And even if by mistake he took the head tefillin first, he should put on the hand tefillin first, in order to fulfil the mitzva in its order (Shulḥan Arukh 25:6).

Those who follow the Kabbala put on the hand tefillin sitting and the head tefillin standing, and those who follow the Rema put on both standing (Rema 25:11; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 33).

It is forbidden to interrupt with speech or with a gesture between putting on the hand tefillin and the head tefillin, for their fulfilment must be as one, and one who interrupts between them commits a transgression (Sota 44a-b; Menaḥot 36a). Therefore, immediately after winding the straps of the hand tefillin on the arm, and even before winding them properly on the fingers, one hurries to put on the head tefillin, and after finishing putting on the head tefillin one finishes winding the straps of the hand tefillin (Mishna Berura 25:29; 38; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 70).

However, in a case of circumstances beyond his control, when he has only one tefilla, hand or head, he should put on the tefilla he has. And likewise one who has a wound at the place of the tefillin on his head or arm should put on the tefillin he is able to put on. For the mitzvot of putting on the hand tefillin and the head tefillin are two mitzvot that do not hold each other back (Menaḥot 38a; Shulḥan Arukh 26:1; Mishna Berura 1).

The meaning of the matter is that the hand tefillin are meant to bind our heart to the service of God, whereas the head tefillin are meant to bind our mind to faith in God, and one must take care not to create a separation and disconnection between the mind and the heart. For one of the hard problems in human life is the separation between the mind and the heart: the mind understands one way and the heart wants otherwise. But when there is no choice, when only one side is meanwhile able to draw near to the service of God, it should draw near, because each value on its own is also important.

If he heard Kaddish or Kedusha between putting on the hand tefillin and the head tefillin, he should not respond, but be silent and concentrate (Shulḥan Arukh 25:10).

sections.title_en: 11. The Blessing over the Tefillin
sections.body_en:
Over putting on the hand tefillin one recites: "Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to put on tefillin." And the poskim disagreed whether one must recite a further blessing over putting on the head tefillin.

For those who follow the 'Shulḥan Arukh', since these are two mitzvot whose purpose is one, the blessing over the hand tefillin serves for the head tefillin too, and there is no need to add a special blessing for them. Only one who interrupted with speech between putting on the hand tefillin and putting on the head tefillin must recite over the head tefillin "al mitzvat tefillin" (concerning the mitzva of tefillin).

And for those who follow the Rema, since these are two mitzvot, one must add a blessing over putting on the head tefillin: "Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us concerning the mitzva of tefillin", and if he interrupted between them with speech, he must recite both blessings over the head tefillin. Out of respect for those who hold that one should not recite a blessing over the head tefillin, people are accustomed, after tightening the straps, to say 'Barukh shem kevod malkhuto le-olam va-ed' (Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever).11

For all the mitzvot one must recite the blessing as close as possible to their performance (Menaḥot 35b). And since the mitzva is to 'bind' the tefillin on the hand and the head, one must recite the blessing close to the binding. That is, one should not recite the blessing after taking the tefillin out of the bag, since that is not truly close to the performance of the mitzva. Nor should one recite the blessing after binding the tefillin on the arm, since the mitzva has already been done. Rather, one should first put the hand tefillin in its place and hold it with the hand while tightening the strap, recite the blessing, and fasten the tefillin by winding the strap around the arm. For winding the strap is the binding, since without the winding the hand tefilla does not stay in its place (Shulḥan Arukh 25:8). And likewise for those who follow the Rema and recite a blessing over putting on the head tefillin, the time of the blessing is after placing the straps on the head and before tightening them, for in the tightening the mitzva of binding is done.

One who removes the tefillin intending to put them on again should not recite the blessing again, since he has not diverted his attention from them. But if he intended to remove them for more than half an hour, when he puts them on again he should recite the blessing again. And likewise if he removed them in order to relieve himself in the lavatory or to pass wind, even though he removed them for a short time, since he was obligated to remove them, when he puts them on again he should recite the blessing again (see Rema 25:12; Mishna Berura 47).12

notes_en.en:
The basis of the dispute is in the explanation of the Gemara in Menaḥot (36a), where it is explained that if one interrupted between putting on the hand and head tefillin one must recite a blessing, and it is further explained that there are two blessings: 'le-haniaḥ' for the hand tefillin and 'al mitzvat' for the head tefillin. According to the Rif, the Rambam, the Rashba and others, in an ordinary situation one recites one blessing, and only when one interrupted must one add the blessing over the head tefillin. Whereas according to Rabbeinu Tam, Rabbeinu Yona, the Rosh and others, in every case one recites a blessing over the head tefillin, and what they said, that if one interrupted one adds a blessing, means that one recites two blessings over putting on the head tefillin, 'le-haniaḥ tefillin' and 'al mitzvat tefillin' (Shulḥan Arukh and Rema 25:9). Although most of those of Ashkenazi origin follow the Rema, some follow the Shulḥan Arukh, and they are those who follow the Gra (25:7) and the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 23. The Rema wrote, based on Mahari Ibn Ḥaviv, that it is good to say after finishing tightening the head tefillin: "Barukh shem kevod malkhuto le-olam va-ed", as one says after a blessing said by mistake. And although according to their custom there is no mistake in this, they say it out of respect for the view of those who disagree. In addition, this saying contains an added acceptance of the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven, which is a fitting continuation of putting on the head tefillin (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 25:13). And some are not accustomed to say it (Levush 25:6, based on Eliya Rabba Zuta; Shulḥan Ha-Tahor 25:4).
If he heard Kaddish or Kedusha between putting on the hand and head tefillin, he should not respond, but be silent and concentrate (Shulḥan Arukh 25:10). And if he responded, according to the Rosh and the Rashba he has interrupted and must add a blessing for the head tefillin. And so wrote the Magen Avraham 17, Eliya Rabba 14, Ḥayei Adam (13:5), Mishna Berura 36. And some say that after the fact words of holiness are not considered an interruption (the Mordekhai in the name of Rabbeinu Tam), and many took this view into account and ruled that if he responded he should not add a blessing. So wrote the Taz (25:8), Ma'amar Mordekhai 9, Ḥesed La-Alafim 8, Shetilei Zeitim 20, Ben Ish Ḥai (Vayera 10), Yabi'a Omer (9, Oraḥ Ḥayim 82:1).
One who puts on only the hand tefillin recites 'le-haniaḥ'. And one who puts on only the head tefillin: for those accustomed to recite one blessing, he recites only 'al mitzvat' (Shulḥan Arukh 26:2), and those accustomed to recite two blessings recite both blessings (Rema there; Mishna Berura 2).

According to the Shulḥan Arukh (25:12), even one who removes tefillin intending to put them back immediately should recite the blessing. On the other hand, the Ben Ish Ḥai wrote (Vayera 13) that even if he removed the tefillin in order to enter the lavatory, when he puts them on again he should say the blessing without the Name and kingship, in order to take into account the views that one need not recite the blessing. But the view of most poskim is as explained above, and as the Rema (25:12), the Mishna Berura 47 and Yabi'a Omer (8, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2, note at the end) wrote. And as we learned regarding tzitzit, above 1:6, note 7. If he forgot to recite the blessing when putting on the tefillin, as long as the tefillin are on him he may recite it, and as soon as he remembers that he did not recite the blessing over the tefillin he should touch them and recite the blessing (Mishna Berura 25:26).

sections.title_en: 12. Removing the Tefillin
sections.body_en:
One removes the head tefillin first and afterwards the hand tefillin, the reverse of the order in which they were put on (Menaḥot 36a). Out of respect for the Torah scroll, from the time the Torah scroll is taken out until it is returned to the ark one should not remove tefillin in its presence. And one who needs to remove tefillin should turn to another side so as not to remove the tefillin facing it (Mishna Berura 25:58). Similarly, out of respect for one's rabbi, a person should not remove his tefillin in the presence of his principal teacher, and if he needs to remove the tefillin he should turn to another side so as not to remove the tefillin facing him (Shulḥan Arukh 38:11).

Ideally people are accustomed not to remove the tefillin before the end of the Kaddish after 'U-va le-Tziyon', and on Mondays and Thursdays, when the Torah is read, according to the Sephardi custom one waits until after the Torah scroll is returned to the ark (Shulḥan Arukh 25:13). And some are accustomed to enhance the mitzva and wait until after the first Mourner's Kaddish (Rema; Mishna Berura 56). And some are accustomed to enhance it and wait until the end of everything said at the conclusion of the morning prayer. Out of respect for the Kaddish, whose standing is great, ideally one should not remove the tefillin during the Kaddish (Mishna Berura 56).

sections.title_en: 13. The Time of Tefillin During the Day, and the Law of a Mourner on the First Day
sections.body_en:
From the Torah the time for the mitzva of putting on tefillin is by day and by night, but the Sages decreed not to put on tefillin at night, lest one forget and fall asleep with them on and pass wind in his sleep, and so be found treating the tefillin with contempt (Shulḥan Arukh 30:2). Therefore, one who wears tefillin during the day should remove them before the emergence of the stars (Mishna Berura 15).

The Sages established that the time for beginning to put on tefillin in the morning is the same as the time of the mitzva of tzitzit, that is, from when the dawn grows light enough that one can distinguish between tekhelet and white, which is the time called 'mi-she-yakir' (Berakhot 9b; above 1:9; Peninei Halakha, Tefilla 11, note 2). One who needs to set out on a journey and to begin praying before that in the synagogue, or one who intends to pray on the way but will not be able to take off his coat in order to put on tefillin, should put them on beforehand, and when the time of 'mi-she-yakir' arrives he should touch the tefillin and recite the blessing over them (Shulḥan Arukh 30:3; Peninei Halakha there 11:8).

Even one who because of circumstances beyond his control or forgetfulness did not put on tefillin during the day should not put them on at night. But if it is not yet truly night but only bein ha-shemashot (twilight), which is doubtfully day and doubtfully night, he should put them on without a blessing.13

Although a mourner is obligated in all the mitzvot, he may not put on tefillin on the first day, because the tefillin are called 'pe'er' (glory), and the mourner on the first day, which is especially bitter, is considered as one whose ashes (efer) are on his head, and one may not place the glory where ashes are fitting (Berakhot 11a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 38:5; Yoreh De'ah 388:1).14

notes_en.en:
Tannaim and Amoraim disagreed whether from the Torah there is a mitzva to put on tefillin at night. According to Rabbi Yosi Ha-Gelili, from the Torah the time of tefillin is by day only, as it is said (Shemot 13:10): "You shall keep this statute in its season from year to year (mi-yamim yamima)" – days and not nights. And so the Rambam ruled (Tefillin 4:10). And in the view of Rabbi Akiva, this verse was said about the Pesaḥ offering, and from the Torah the time of tefillin is also at night, except that because of the concern that people might fall asleep in them and they would be treated with contempt, the Sages decreed not to put them on at night. And this is the view of almost all the Rishonim, because the conclusion of the Gemara is according to Rav Ashi, that from the Torah the time of tefillin is also at night and only by rabbinic law are they not put on at night (the Terumah, the Rid, the Or Zarua, the Semag, the Rashba, the Rosh and many others; and so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh 30:2).
However, one who put on tefillin and the emergence of the stars arrived is not obligated to remove them until he goes to sleep, except that this is "the halakha, but we do not rule so". Therefore only one who is alone may remain with the tefillin after the emergence of the stars. And if he relieves himself and needs to remove them, he should not put them on again (Menaḥot 36a-b; Shulḥan Arukh 30:2; Mishna Berura 6; 8). One who has not put on tefillin should put them on until the emergence of the stars. Above I wrote that he should then put them on without a blessing, according to the view of the Bi'ur Halakha (30:5, s.v. 'Yesh') and Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 17. However, some say that since by the letter of the law the night is a time for tefillin, during bein ha-shemashot he should put them on with a blessing (Ḥayei Adam 14:16; Artzot Ha-Ḥayim 30:2; Halikhot Olam, Ḥayei Sara 3).

In the view of the great majority of poskim, even when the burial was not on the day of death, it is forbidden to put on tefillin on the first day of the shiva. So wrote the Eliya Rabba (38:2), Maḥazik Berakha (1-2), Mishna Berura 16, Dagul Me-Revava (Yoreh De'ah 388:1), Rabbi Akiva Eiger there, Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 3, Kaf Ha-Ḥayim (Palagi 10:37), Ben Ish Ḥai (Ḥayei Sara 12), Kitzur Shulḥan Arukh (211:2-3), Gesher Ha-Ḥayim (1, 18:4), and many others. However, some say that if the burial was on the day after the day of death, one should put on tefillin after the burial (Maharit Tz 14; Ma'amar Mordekhai 38:4). And some say that it is fitting to take their view into account and put them on discreetly without a blessing (Yabi'a Omer 2, Yoreh De'ah 27; Halikhot Shlomo 18:5). In practice, one should follow the view of the great majority of poskim, who forbade putting them on, but one who very much wants to put them on may put them on discreetly without a blessing.

sections.title_en: 14. Shabbat and Yom Tov
sections.body_en:
On Shabbat and Yom Tov it is forbidden to put on tefillin, because the tefillin are meant to be a sign of our bond with the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Shemot 13:9): "And it shall be for a sign to you upon your hand", and Shabbat and Yom Tov too are called a sign, as it is said (there 31:13): "It is a sign between Me and you" (Menaḥot 36b; Shulḥan Arukh 31:1). That is, both the tefillin and Shabbatot and festivals are meant to express the special bond between the Holy One, blessed be He, and Israel. If so, on Shabbat and Yom Tov, when through the holiness of the day there is already a sign of our bond with the Holy One, blessed be He, there is no need to put on tefillin. Moreover, some say that one who puts on tefillin on Shabbat and Yom Tov testifies about himself that he does not understand the meaning of the holiness of Shabbat and Yom Tov, and therefore it is forbidden to put on tefillin on them (Shulḥan Arukh and Levush 31:1).15 Since it is forbidden to put them on, they are muktzeh, and it is forbidden to move them on Shabbat, according to the law of 'a vessel whose function is for a forbidden purpose'. However, in a pressing situation, when the tefillin might be damaged, it is permitted to move them in order to save them (Peninei Halakha, Shabbat, and Harḥavot 23:8).

Regarding the days of Ḥol Ha-Mo'ed the Rishonim disagreed. Some say that since some melakhot are permitted on them, they are not considered a 'sign', and one is obligated to put on tefillin on them, and so many in Ashkenaz were accustomed (the Rosh, the Rema). And some say that the prohibition of ḥametz on Ḥol Ha-Mo'ed Pesaḥ and the mitzva to dwell in the sukka on Ḥol Ha-Mo'ed Sukkot are the 'sign' of the bond between the Holy One, blessed be He, and Israel, and in order not to belittle the 'sign' of the festivals, it is forbidden to put on tefillin on Ḥol Ha-Mo'ed too (the Rashba; Shulḥan Arukh 31:2). And so they were accustomed in Sepharad, and so some of the Jews of Ashkenaz were accustomed. In practice, abroad it is right for every community to continue its custom, but in the Land of Israel the members of all communities are accustomed not to put on tefillin, and so all who immigrate to the Land must act (see Peninei Halakha, Mo'adim 10, note 1).

On Rosh Ḥodesh tefillin are put on, but since it has holiness, people are accustomed to remove the tefillin before the Musaf prayer (Shulḥan Arukh 25:13), for the Musaf prayer of Rosh Ḥodesh is like Yom Tov. It is right to wait until one has finished winding the tefillin in their straps and putting them in the bag, and only afterwards to begin the silent Musaf, for otherwise the tefillin would lie disrespectfully during the Musaf prayer (see Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 1:14, note 19).

notes_en.en: Rabbeinu Baḥya wrote (Bereshit 17:24) that three mitzvot are a sign and testimony of the faith of Israel: circumcision, Shabbat and tefillin. And there must always be two signs. On weekdays they are circumcision and tefillin, and on Shabbat and Yom Tov, Shabbat and circumcision. And so wrote the Semag and the Levush (29:1). The Shakh (Yoreh De'ah 265:24) and the Magen Avraham (Oraḥ Ḥayim 25:28) wrote that when a berit mila is after the prayer, people are accustomed to remain in tefillin, because they are a sign like the circumcision. Thus far. Some ask: why is this not a superfluous sign, as on Shabbat? The Eliya Rabba (29:1) explained in the name of the Rokeaḥ that the sign of circumcision is not a remembrance of the exodus from Egypt, and therefore it is good to join another sign to it, but tefillin and Shabbat and Yom Tov are a remembrance of the exodus from Egypt, and therefore they should not be kept together. And according to what we learned from Rabbeinu Baḥya and the Semag, there is no question, for it is good that there be two signs and not three. And so wrote the Ḥida (Mar'it Ha-Ayin, Likkutim 2).

sections.title_en: 15. The Prohibition of Diverting One's Attention
sections.body_en:
Throughout the time the tefillin are worn it is forbidden to divert one's attention from them, for the Sages learned (Menaḥot 36b) from the tzitz on the head of the High Priest, on which the Name of God is mentioned only once, and the Torah commanded (Shemot 28:38): "And it shall be upon his forehead always" – that he not divert his attention from it; all the more so it is forbidden to divert one's attention from the tefillin, in which the Names of God are mentioned twenty-one times. Therefore the Sages ruled (there): "A person is obligated to touch his tefillin at every moment", so that he will not divert his attention from them. And he should touch the hand tefillin first and afterwards the head tefillin, because the hand tefillin are closer to his hand, and one does not pass over mitzvot (Shulḥan Arukh 28:1; Mishna Berura 3). However, during prayer and study he is not obligated to touch them, because through the intention of his heart in prayer or study he directs his heart to God (Mishna Berura 44:3, and Bi'ur Halakha there). Yet even during study and prayer it is good to touch them from time to time, in order to make sure that they have not moved from their place.

Included in the prohibition of diverting one's attention while wearing tefillin is that it is forbidden to entertain thoughts of desire for a forbidden woman (Shulḥan Arukh 38:4). It is likewise forbidden to enter a state of laughter and levity. And likewise one who is so preoccupied with bodily thoughts or with his distress that he entirely diverts his attention from his faith in God or from his service should not put on tefillin (see Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 28:1). But one who is engaged in his work and is not thinking about the fact that he is wearing tefillin is not considered as diverting his attention, for there is no contradiction between wearing tefillin and engaging in the settlement of the world; but he should touch them from time to time so that he will remember the tefillin (Rabbeinu Yona; Rosh, Berakhot 3:28).

And some are stringent and hold that one who wears tefillin must remember at every moment that the tefillin are on him, and that not more than the time it takes to walk a hundred amot (about a minute) should pass without his remembering that the tefillin are on him (Sha'agat Arye 39). But the view of most poskim is not so. As is proven from the fact that the prohibition of sleeping in tefillin is only because of the concern lest one pass wind in them, and therefore by the letter of the law it is permitted to take a short nap in them in a way that there is no concern that he will pass wind in them or be drawn into a regular sleep (Sukka 26a; Shulḥan Arukh 44:1).16

notes_en.en:
