The Sages learned in Menaḥot (36b) the prohibition of diverting one's attention and the mitzva to touch the tefillin by a kal va-ḥomer from the tzitz. From the words of the Rambam it is implied that it is a complete kal va-ḥomer, while according to Tosafot (Yoma 8a) it is not a complete kal va-ḥomer, since it can be refuted: the Name on the tzitz is exposed, whereas the Names in the tefillin are hidden.
Shulḥan Arukh (38:4): "One who puts on tefillin must beware of thoughts of desire for a woman. Gloss: and if it is impossible for him without such thoughts, it is better not to put them on." The source of the words of the Rema is in the Kol Bo, who wrote in the name of the Maharam that young men who cannot avoid such thoughts even during the recitation of Shema should not put on tefillin. And so it is implied by the Yerushalmi (Berakhot 2:3), that the clean body required for tefillin is also "from an evil thought" (Beit Yosef 38:4). And it appears that there is no prohibition against thinking of one's wife, and therefore the discussion was about young men who are not married. And so it is proven from Sukka (26b), that it is forbidden to sleep by day with tefillin when one's wife is with him, because of the young who may come to 'the familiar thing' (marital relations); and if thinking of one's wife were forbidden, they would have had to say lest they come to such thoughts; rather, thinking of one's wife is not forbidden and is not considered diverting one's attention. And so it emerges from the Beit Yosef, who concluded the discussion with the words of the Yerushalmi, that the prohibition is 'in a forbidden thought'. And so wrote the Olat Tamid 5 and Mishna Berura 14.
In the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (28:1) he defined that the prohibition of diverting attention is "when one stands in laughter or levity (based on Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona and the Rosh, Berakhot 3:28), or one's mind is so preoccupied with bodily needs that his heart turns away from the fear of Heaven because of his preoccupation. But when one stands in awe and is occupied with his needs, even though he is engaged in his craft and his mind is not actually on the tefillin, this is not called diverting attention, for if it were otherwise how could every person go about in tefillin all day. In any case, it is the choicest form of the mitzva not to divert one's attention from them at all, except during Torah study and the Shemoneh Esreh prayer."
The law of one in distress regarding tefillin: the Shulḥan Arukh wrote (38:9): "One in distress, and one whose mind is not settled and composed, is exempt, because it is forbidden to divert one's attention from them." The intention is one who is so occupied with his distress that he cannot direct his mind to faith or to service. However, if he can settle his mind for one moment, he is obligated to settle his mind and fulfil the mitzva of tefillin; this is the view of many poskim, and so wrote the Mishna Berura (38:31). And although according to the Beit Yosef, based on R. Manoaḥ, he is not obligated to settle his mind, even in his view there is no prohibition against settling his mind and fulfilling the mitzva (Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 38:30-31). Therefore he must settle his mind and put on tefillin.

sections.title_en: 16. Passing Wind and the Lavatory
sections.body_en:
Since the tefillin are holy, one who wears tefillin must take great care of their honour, as the Sages said (Shabbat 49a): "Tefillin require a clean body, like Elisha Ba'al Kenafayim", who was particular about the honour of the tefillin. The Sages explained that the care required is that one not pass wind in them, so that the tefillin would be treated with great contempt. And they were so concerned about harm to the honour of the tefillin that although from the Torah the mitzva of tefillin applies at night as by day, the Sages instituted not to put them on at night, lest one fall asleep while they are on him and pass wind in them (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 30:2; above note 13). All the more so it is forbidden to relieve oneself in the lavatory while they are on him.

Not only this, but since the Rishonim saw that if Israel were accustomed to wear tefillin all day, many would stumble from time to time by passing wind in tefillin, as well as by forbidden diversion of attention, they ruled not to wear tefillin all day but only at the time of prayer (Rosh; Maharaḥ Or Zarua; Semak; Shulḥan Arukh 37:2; above halakha 3). In this way they moved from a period in which people strengthened their faith by wearing tefillin all day despite the stumbling involved, to a period in which they strengthened their faith by emphasising the honour of the tefillin.

One who dozes lightly during the morning prayer is not obligated to remove them, but it is forbidden to take even a short nap in them, lest he pass wind in them (see Shulḥan Arukh 44:1; Mishna Berura 4-7).17

notes_en.en:
According to the Sha'agat Arye 40, the prohibition of passing wind in tefillin is from the Torah, because of contempt for a mitzva, which the Sages learned (Shabbat 22a) from what is said, "and he shall pour out and cover", that one should not cover the blood with the foot, so that mitzvot will not be contemptible to him (and so wrote Zera Emet 3:5). On the other hand, many hold that the prohibition is rabbinic, because this foul smell has no substance (Responsa Rema 98; Peri Megadim, Mishbetzot Zahav 80:1; Mishna Berura 4). In addition, it is possible that contempt for a mitzva itself is forbidden by rabbinic law and the derivation is an asmakhta (Rosh Yosef, Shabbat 22a; Darkhei Teshuva 26:51, in the name of the Ran and the Yam Shel Shlomo).
In the Eshel Avraham (Buczacz 38:2) he leans to hold that the main prohibition of passing wind is in making a sound or a noticeable foul smell, as is considered disgraceful before a king, but without this it is a light prohibition, and even according to the Sha'agat Arye it is rabbinic. And in Od Yosef Ḥai (Parashat Ḥayei Sara 4) he holds that the prohibition is because of the foul smell, and when there is no foul smell, even if he made a sound, there is no prohibition and no disgrace. Thus far. And so it is implied by the fact that when people went about in tefillin all day, they permitted urinating with tefillin in a temporary lavatory, since there is no concern that as a result he will defecate, which is entirely forbidden; and according to the Rambam it is forbidden lest he pass wind in them (Shulḥan Arukh 43:1). So passing wind is more severe than urinating, and the natural understanding is that it is because of the foul smell and perhaps also the sound.
The Rishonim wrote that the concern of a clean body is the main reason because of which people became accustomed to put on tefillin in the morning prayer only and not all day (Rosh, Tefillin 28; Semak 153). And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh (37:2): "Their mitzva is that they be on him all day, but because they require a clean body, that one not pass wind in them and not divert one's attention from them, and not every person can be careful with them, people became accustomed not to wear them all day. In any case every person must be careful that they be on him during the recitation of Shema and prayer." One can explain that ideally they took into account the view of those who are stringent regarding diversion of attention (the view of the Sha'agat Arye). But it appears more likely that this custom was founded on the view of most poskim, except that if everyone wore tefillin all day there would be many who would transgress from time to time the prohibition of passing wind and of thinking forbidden thoughts, and therefore they became accustomed to be stringent.
One who is ill in his bowels and constantly needs to relieve himself, or cannot hold back from passing wind even for a few seconds, should not put on tefillin (Shulḥan Arukh 38:1). And if he can hold back for a few seconds, he should put on tefillin and remove them immediately. And if he can hold back for a few more seconds, he should also say the first verse of the recitation of Shema in them (Shulḥan Arukh 38:2). Likewise, one who cannot hold back from passing wind during the Amida prayer should not pray the Amida (Shulḥan Arukh 80:1), because the Amida prayer is like standing before a king. But other words of holiness he should say, since they are not considered as standing before the king (see Peninei Halakha, Tefilla 5:8-10). Therefore he should wrap himself in a tallit and say the morning blessings and the recitation of Shema and its blessings (Mishna Berura 38:7). And whenever he smells a foul smell he should stop saying blessings (Shulḥan Arukh 79:9). And if he sprays the place with a fragrant substance that masks the foul smell, he may continue saying the blessings without interruption, and only at the moment of passing wind itself should he stop (Ben Ish Ḥai, Bo 28). And many hold that even one who cannot avoid passing wind should pray the Amida (Mekor Ḥayim by the author of the Ḥavot Ya'ir; Mor U-Ketzi'a; the Gra; Mega'ale Gevurot, and others). And some hold that he should even put on tefillin for one moment, because the prohibition of passing wind is rabbinic, and one should not on its account neglect the Torah mitzva of putting on tefillin (Mor U-Ketzi'a, Oraḥ Ḥayim 80; Peri Megadim, Mishbetzot Zahav 1).

sections.title_en: 17. Care Not to Treat the Tefillin with Contempt
sections.body_en:
Out of respect for the tefillin, it is forbidden to enter a lavatory or a bathhouse with them, whether a person is wearing them or they are in his hand. However, in the time when people were accustomed to wear tefillin all day, they sometimes needed to be lenient about this out of concern that the tefillin would be stolen. But when they were at home, they were careful not to enter the lavatory with the tefillin (Shulḥan Arukh 43:7; Mishna Berura 24).

One who is on his way with the tefillin in his hand or in his rucksack and needs to go into a toilet should, if possible, leave them with a friend and go into the toilet. And if that is not possible, he may go into the toilet with the rucksack, because the tefillin are hidden in a bag within a bag, the second bag, that is, the rucksack, not being their usual bag (Maḥatzit Ha-Shekel; Mishna Berura 43:24). He may likewise put the tefillin bag in a plastic bag and so go into the toilet.

One who puts tefillin in a rucksack or a suitcase should put them above the clothes and objects there, but if his aim is to protect them he may put them between the clothes and objects. One may put on the ground the rucksack or suitcase in which the tefillin are, but he should not sit on them or put his feet on them, unless they are large and he knows that the tefillin are on the other side (Shulḥan Arukh 40:3; 5; see Mishna Berura 13).18

While wearing tefillin it is fitting not to touch covered parts of the body or shoes in a way that requires washing the hands afterwards, and when necessary it is permitted (Mekor Ḥayim by the author of the Ḥavot Ya'ir 43:9).

Israel are accustomed that if a person mistakenly dropped the hand or head tefillin on the ground, he fasts for one day (Magen Avraham 44:5; Mishna Berura 40:3). Today people are accustomed to fast less, and instead they give to charity the amount that the person would be willing to pay so as not to have to fast for one day. And one for whom it is hard to pay this sum should pay according to the value of the food he eats in one day. If the tefillin fell while they were in their bag, since the harm to their honour is lighter, people were not accustomed to fast, and it is good to give a little charity as a result.19 People try to ensure that the straps too do not touch the floor, and if they touched it they pick them up.

One who stumbled and, while the tefillin were on him, passed wind and made a foul smell, it is right that he fast for it that whole day, for passing wind is considered more serious contempt than dropping tefillin (Eshel Avraham of Buczacz 38:2). But as said, today people are accustomed to redeem the fast with charity in the amount he would have been willing to pay so as not to fast.

notes_en.en: It is further explained in the Shulḥan Arukh (40:1) that it is forbidden to hang the tefillin housings on a hook, or even to hold them hanging in one's hand, whether the housing is below or the knot of the tefillin is below. But when he comes to put on the tefillin, it is permitted to hold the straps, even though the housing and the knot hang in the air, because it is for a second and for the purpose of putting them on (Mishna Berura 40:2). And some enhance the mitzva by holding the housing and the knot and so putting them on the head (Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 40:1).

The custom to fast is brought in the Aḥaronim in the name of Responsa Mahari Bruna 127 and Mishpetei Shmuel 12. And the intention is that he fasts on the very day it fell, even though he did not accept the fast upon himself beforehand (Mahari Bruna; Eliya Rabba 40:5; Ḥesed La-Alafim 44:5; unlike Kaf Ha-Ḥayim of Palagi 10:38). The Ḥida wrote (Ḥayim She'al 1:12) that if the fast is hard for him, or he is a Torah scholar whose learning will suffer because of the fast, he should redeem it with charity. And so wrote the Ben Ish Ḥai (Ḥayei Sara 18). Today the custom is to redeem it with charity, as explained above. And in addition, it is good to add an hour of Torah study (see Hagahot Mahari Bruna there).
The Mahari Bruna wrote there that his teachers hold that even if the tefillin fell while in their case one must fast, but in his view it is enough to give a peruta to charity. And so the Aḥaronim agreed, among them the Ben Ish Ḥai and the Mishna Berura. One who sees tefillin that fell need not fast at all (Mishpetei Shmuel and Ḥayim She'al there).

sections.title_en: 18. Drinking and Eating
sections.body_en:
Since one must take care of the honour of the tefillin, a drunk person who is not capable of speaking with the honour fitting before the King may not put on tefillin. And the Sages even forbade eating a regular meal in them, lest he become drunk and behave disgracefully and so be found treating them with contempt (Rashi, Berakhot 23b). But casual eating is permitted, since there is no concern that he will be drawn into drunkenness (Shulḥan Arukh 40:8). Today, when we are accustomed to enhance the sanctity of the tefillin by wearing them only in the morning prayer and the learning after it, it is right not to eat even casually in them (Shulḥan Shlomo 40:6; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 5). However, one who after the morning prayer is accustomed to learn at length with the tefillin may taste a little and drink in order to strengthen himself in his learning.20

In the past, when the feasting around a wedding continued for days and nights, the Sages ruled that the groom and his companions are exempt from putting on tefillin and from prayer during the days of feasting, since they are accustomed to drink wine and to be in a light-headed state. And they did not argue against them that they should not drink, because they were engaged in the great mitzva of gladdening the groom and bride, and one engaged in a mitzva is exempt from planning how he will fulfil another mitzva. However, they were obligated in the recitation of Shema, because it requires intention only in the first verse (Sukka 25b; the Rid and the Meiri). And presumably at that moment they would also put on tefillin, so as not to appear to bear false witness. But they did not wear tefillin all day as they were accustomed in those times, nor did they pray the Amida prayer, which requires seriousness (Responsa Rema 132). Today, when people are accustomed to limit the time of the feasting at night, and by the time of the morning prayer the companions are no longer drunk, the companions are obligated to put on tefillin and pray the whole morning prayer (Mishna Berura 38:23). And even the groom himself is obligated in the recitation of Shema, prayer and tefillin (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 70:3; Mishna Berura 38:23).

notes_en.en: Yerushalmi Berakhot (2:3): "He may eat a casual meal in them, but he may not eat a regular meal in them." And so wrote the Rambam (Tefillin 4:16) and the Shulḥan Arukh (40:8). See Peninei Halakha, Sukkot 3:4, for the definition of casual eating. Rashi explained (Berakhot 23b, s.v. 'Ḥoletz') that one does not eat a regular meal in them "lest he become drunk at the meal and behave disgracefully in his tefillin". All the more so it is forbidden for a drunk person to put on tefillin, and so wrote the Shulḥan Shlomo (40:4). He further wrote there (40:6): "It is permitted to eat casually in tefillin, and it seems to me that this is specifically if he wears them all day, but otherwise it is forbidden." And so wrote the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 5. However, in Responsa Teshurat Shai (first edition 215) he permitted eating casually in them, because we should not make decrees of our own (although he testified about himself that he never did so). And so emerges from the Mekor Ḥayim (by the author of the Ḥavot Ya'ir 40:8). Above I wrote that it is right to be stringent, because today we are accustomed to be more stringent in the laws of the sanctity of the tefillin, and only one who remains in tefillin after the prayer may taste a little as needed. And so wrote Responsa Lev Avraham (Weinfeld 1:5).

sections.title_en: 19. From When a Minor Begins to Put On Tefillin
sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Sukka 42a) of a minor who knows "how to look after tefillin – his father acquires tefillin for him". The intention is from when the minor knows how to guard the sanctity of the tefillin, so that throughout the time he wears them he will not sleep, will not pass wind and will not divert his attention to matters of laughter and mockery. However, over the generations Israel became accustomed to enhance more the guarding of the honour and sanctity of the tefillin, and just as adults wear tefillin only in the morning prayer and the learning close to it, so too there is concern about training minors in tefillin before the time of their obligation, lest they fail to guard their honour properly.

The prevalent custom is to train children to put on tefillin about one to three months before the bar mitzva. And some of those of Sephardi and Yemenite origin are accustomed to train responsible children a year or two before the bar mitzva. And some of those of Ashkenazi origin are accustomed to begin putting on tefillin on the day of the bar mitzva, and before that they teach them how to put them on but do not accustom them to put on tefillin at the morning prayer.

Ideally it is fitting for every person to act according to the custom of his forefathers, but if the father sees that it is more suitable for his son to bring forward the time of putting on tefillin, or to delay it until the bar mitzva, he should do what suits his son.21

Some say that it is right for a youth to recite 'She-heḥeyanu' when he begins putting on tefillin for the first time. But in practice one should not recite 'She-heḥeyanu' over them, since this is the view of many, and this is the prevalent custom. Parents who want their son who is beginning to put on tefillin to recite 'She-heḥeyanu' should buy him a new garment, and so he can recite the blessing over the garment and have the tefillin in mind as well.22

notes_en.en:
In Sukka (42a): "A minor who knows… how to look after tefillin – his father acquires tefillin for him." Knows how to look after them means that he will not pass wind in them (the Semak, the Terumah), and likewise that he will not divert his attention to forbidden matters. Plainly, the law of training applies to each mitzva according to its nature, as the baraita details there regarding tzitzit and lulav; and so wrote the Beit Yosef (37:2). Some wrote that training in the mitzva of tefillin is around the ages of 9-10 (Knesset Ha-Gedola, Hagahot Beit Yosef 37:2; Shulḥan Gavo'ah 5; Shetilei Zeitim 6; and so many in North Africa were accustomed). And some wrote even from the age of 6-7 (Mayim Ḥayim of Messas 2:351), and some wrote about a year or two before the age of bar mitzva (Yabi'a Omer 6, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3).
However, the Ittur learned, based on the Mekhilta, "and you shall keep (ve-shamarta) this statute": I spoke only of one who knows how to look after tefillin, but a minor who does not know how to look after his tefillin is exempt from tefillin. The Ittur explained: "And it seems to us that this 'minor' is an adult of thirteen years… and the Mishna that teaches that minors are exempt from tefillin is speaking of adults who do not know how to look after them." Based on his words, the Rema wrote that the custom is that minors do not put on tefillin "until they are bar mitzva, that is, thirteen years and one day" (Darkhei Moshe 37:3; Rema there). But after the age of thirteen the Rema ruled like the other poskim and not like the Ittur (Bi'ur Halakha, s.v. 'De-hai katan'). And so wrote many poskim, that people are accustomed to put on tefillin close to the bar mitzva. Some wrote about two or three months before (Magen Avraham 37:4; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav 3; Ḥayei Adam 66:2; Mishna Berura 37:8), some wrote a month (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 4), and some wrote that one should not put them on before the day of the bar mitzva (Shulḥan Ha-Tahor 37:4). And some Ashkenazi poskim disagreed with the Rema and agreed with the Shulḥan Arukh (Baḥ 4; Olat Tamid). And the Shela explained that it may be that in our time, when people are accustomed to put on tefillin only at the time of prayer, the Ittur too would agree that a minor may put them on several years before the bar mitzva. And similarly wrote the Sefat Emet (Sukka 42a). Therefore, if the parents see that it suits their son to put on tefillin about a year or two before the bar mitzva, they may act so.

Menaḥot 75b: "If he was standing and offering menaḥot in Jerusalem, he says: Blessed is He who has kept us alive and sustained us." Rashi explained that this refers to a kohen offering for the first time in his life. And so wrote the Rokeaḥ (371), that over a mitzva a person performs for the first time in his life he should recite 'She-heḥeyanu'. And so wrote the Rema, Yoreh De'ah 28:2, that one who covers the blood of a wild animal or bird for the first time should recite 'She-heḥeyanu'. And so wrote many regarding tzitzit and tefillin (the Baḥ; Taz, Oraḥ Ḥayim 22:1; Eliya Rabba 2; Artzot Ha-Ḥayim 1, and others). However, the prevalent custom is not to recite it, and the Tevu'ot Shor explained (Yoreh De'ah 28:4) that this is because people are accustomed to put on tefillin before the bar mitzva, and 'She-heḥeyanu' was not instituted for the stage of training. And so wrote the Eshel Avraham of Buczacz (37:3) and the Tzitz Eliezer (13:24). And some say that one should not recite 'She-heḥeyanu' at all on performing a mitzva for the first time, and the kohanim recited it because it was a mitzva that recurred from time to time according to the time of the kohanim's watch (Tosafot, Berakhot 37b, s.v. 'Haya'; Shakh, Yoreh De'ah 28:5; Peri Ḥadash; Knesset Ha-Gedola, and others).

sections.title_en: 20. Women and Tefillin
sections.body_en: Women are exempt from the mitzva of putting on tefillin, since women are exempt from time-bound positive commandments, and the mitzva of tefillin depends on time, for on weekdays it is a mitzva to put on tefillin, and on Shabbatot and festivals there is no mitzva to put on tefillin (above halakha 14; see Peninei Halakha, Tefillat Nashim 2:7). Regarding other time-bound positive commandments, such as lulav and shofar, there is a virtue for women who perform them, because although they are not obligated in time-bound positive commandments, they have optional mitzvot. But regarding tefillin, even righteous women were not accustomed to put them on, and this is because Israel were accustomed to be very concerned for the honour of the tefillin; therefore even men, who ought properly to wear tefillin all day, are accustomed, because of the concern about harming their honour, to wear them only in the morning prayer in order to fulfil the obligation of the mitzva and no more. And women, who are not obligated in the mitzva, had better not put them on (Magen Avraham; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan). Therefore, a woman who wants to rise higher in mitzvot and comes to ask whether it is good for her to put on tefillin is instructed not to put them on. And if nevertheless she longs and wants to put them on, she has someone to rely on. But it is right that she not put them on in public, because of arrogance.23

notes_en.en:
In the Mishna in Berakhot (20a) it is explained that women are exempt from tefillin. In Eruvin (96a) a baraita is brought: "Mikhal the daughter of Kushi (Shaul) used to put on tefillin, and the Sages did not protest against her." The Rashba (Eruvin there) explained, based on what emerges from the sugya in the Gemara, that women may put on tefillin even ideally. However, in the Yerushalmi Berakhot (2:3), after an anonymous view was brought that the Sages did not protest against Mikhal the daughter of Shaul who put on tefillin, the view of R. Ḥizkiya was brought, that they did protest against her. And Tosafot explained (Eruvin there, s.v. 'Mikhal') the reason of those who hold that they protested against her: because "tefillin require a clean body, and women are not diligent in being careful", and therefore it is not like other time-bound positive commandments, which women were encouraged to fulfil. And some explained that the concern is more general, lest they not be properly careful about their sanctity, including coming to divert their attention (the Ra'avad, the Ran and the Ritva). And perhaps, since women took care of babies and the dirt of the house, they were concerned that they would find it hard to keep their bodies clean (and so emerges from the Yam Shel Shlomo, Kiddushin 1:64). And some say that they protested against women because of the prohibition of 'shall not wear' (lo yilbash) (Yafeh La-Lev 38:2).
In practice, in the view of most Rishonim, the law of tefillin is like the law of other time-bound positive commandments, and women who want to put on tefillin may do so and have a mitzva in it. So wrote the Ḥinukh 421 and the Meiri (Eruvin 96a). And so emerges from the Rambam (Laws of Tzitzit 3:9) and the Rashba (1:123). And so it can be learned from the Behag, the Rif, the Ran and the Ritva, who included the mitzva of tefillin with the other time-bound positive commandments without distinguishing. And so wrote the Shulḥan Arukh anonymously (38:3). And so wrote the Olat Tamid (38:3), that a woman who wants to put on tefillin, if she knows how to keep her body clean, may put them on. And so it was related of several righteous women in earlier and later generations that they were accustomed to put on tefillin, among them the daughters of Rashi and the wife of Rabbi Ḥayim ben Attar.
On the other hand, some of the Rishonim ruled that women should not put on tefillin and protested against those who want to put them on. So wrote the Ra'avad, the Riaz, the Kol Bo 21 in the name of the Maharam of Rothenburg, and Tashbetz Katan 270. And so ruled the great majority of the Aḥaronim, among them: the Yam Shel Shlomo, the Rema (Oraḥ Ḥayim 38:3), Mahariks, Levush 3, Magen Avraham 3, Birkei Yosef (38:1), Peri Megadim (Eshel Avraham 3), Yafeh La-Lev 2, Mishna Berura 13. The Magen Avraham explained (38:3) that if they were obligated in tefillin, the reason that perhaps they would not be careful about cleanliness would not exempt them. But since they are exempt and there is a concern about cleanliness, one should protest so that they do not put them on. Continuing his words, the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan wrote (38:6) that men too find this hard, for tefillin require a clean body like Elisha Ba'al Kenafayim, except that since they are obligated to put on tefillin, they put them on during the recitation of Shema and prayer with maximum care. But women, who are exempt – why should they bring themselves into such a great concern? And the time of the recitation of Shema and prayer is for them like the rest of the day for men.
And so it is accepted to instruct women not to put on tefillin. But one who wants to put them on has something to rely on, though it is right that she put them on discreetly, for since it is not accepted that righteous women put on tefillin, one who puts them on in public appears to be acting proudly. In addition, it is right that the mitzva be done for the sake of Heaven and not in a way that seems intended to promote other aims, such as a struggle for women's equality. In any case one should not protest against a woman who puts on tefillin in public.
It must further be clarified whether during menstruation or at the time of emission of semen the body is considered not clean. From the Olat Tamid 38:3 it is implied somewhat to forbid, for he wrote: "If the woman is old and we know of her that she knows how to keep herself, one should not protest against her." And likewise in the Eshel Avraham of Buczacz (38:1) he raised the possibility that while the menstrual blood is flowing the body is considered not clean. On the other hand, the other Rishonim and Aḥaronim did not mention this concern as a reason why women should not put on tefillin. In any case it appears that when there is an absorbent pad or tampon, the body is considered clean in every situation.
One can perhaps say that tzitzit and tefillin are obligatory mitzvot for men in order to remind them at all times of the foundations of faith and the mitzvot of God, and since women by their nature bind themselves to faith and to cleaving to God more deeply than men, they have no need of this. It is further possible that men were obligated in them in order to remind them of faith and the mitzvot in all their ways, whereas women, who were not accustomed to go out of the house, did not need this. And even when times changed and women began to go out and act in the public sphere as well, their customs of modesty in matters of dress are what guard them and remind them of faith and the mitzvot.
